Whose gold is it anyway...

By: Johann Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Zama zamas... should they be decriminalised or should they go to jail

Unique Selling Point:
Interview with Mayor of Jhb who takes a hard line on people who break the law

Summary:
The past two weeks saw a drama unfold at the original discovery site of the planet's largest gold reef. An unknown number of zamazamas were trapped underground. eventually 3 bodies were retrieved and a number of zamas escaped alive. An unknown number of zamas are presumed to still be hiding inside for fear of persecution when they do come out. Tensions between rescue services and saps on the one side and the zamas on the other opened up a number of questions: What rights do illegal immigrants have when engaged in an illegal activity in our country? should artisanal mining of old and abandoned mines be decriminalised? How do we address this problem? We interview zamas, a relative of the deceased, the director of LRC and also the mayor of Jhb and get vastly different answers

Press Release:


Zama Zamas Trapped
A small group of illegal miners, so-called zama zamas, surfaced from an abandoned mine shaft in Johannesburg this week. They were the lucky ones. Others - some as young as 12 years old - were still stuck in the disused Langlaagte shaft where they had been trapped for two weeks. Search teams recovered the bodies of several miners while others emerged on their own and were later arrested. Carte Blanche asks: who’s responsible for securing Johannesburg’s disused mine shafts to avoid recurring tragedies?


Script:


Zamazamaz

Devi Link
This is Main Reef Road, named after the biggest gold reef on the planet. And this is the spot where they discovered the gold, 130 years ago.

My name is Thabang, I am a zama

Thabang is a zamazama, an illegal miner about to go underground here at Langlaagte, armed only with a cheap headlight, a hammer, a chisel and a bag in which he can carry the ore he wants to bring back. Trips down can take anything from 24 hours to longer than a month, with distances up to 20km's or more crawled to get to the gold. There is no safety gear, and the old disused tunnels are extremely unstable
Thabang
My father and brother knows, they will come and fetch me

On a good trip he can make up to a R1000, but many trips won't yield anything.
At the outbreak of the Anglo/Boer war in 1899 there were already an estimated 150 000 migrant labourers from all over Africa working on the mines, and over the next 100 years many of them started calling Gauteng home. Apartheid and the gold mining era ended roughly at the same time, as most of the gold left over was too expensive to mine for the multinationals. And as one mine after the other shut down, thousands of miners found themselves unemployed, knowing no other way of making a living. Daroh is an ex-zama who knows this spot well. They call the shaft FNB
Daroh
More than 2000 people mine there

And so the zamazamas were born – desperate people going underground trying to get the remaining gold, with crude methods and at great risk to their own safety. With unemployment rife, many newcomers turned into zamas, and when crime syndicates got involved in buying the gold, zamas even started attacking the still operational mines, as South Africa's second gold rush got underway – a classic battle between the haves and the have-nots.



Joburg mayor, Herman Mashaba, has no sympathy for the zamas
Herman
Rule of law

Janet Love is the director of the Legal Resources Centre, and used to be one of the Human Rights' commissioners
Janet
There are 1000's of zamas underground

Emmah, who works as an ore washer with the Zamas, suddenly had a bad dream about this site two weeks ago
Anna
The dream

But hunger does not believe in dreams, and the next day a group of around 30 zamas went down. Leaving their good clothes tied up in plastic bags in this tree they call their locker room, they descended with empty bags and enough water for about 3 days. One of them, 24 year old Sibangani Tsikwa, is Daroh's baby brother and this was his first trip as a zama, against his brother's advice and out of sheer desperation for some money.
Brother


But, once down there, disaster struck. Smoke from an as yet unknown source, overwhelmed the miners
Brother


This was on wednesday, when his brother was already underground for 7 days. He went to the police to beg for help
Brother


No one knew exactly how many miners were still underground, or how many of them were alive.

On friday the rescue services didn't arrive, and the police would not let the relatives and the other zamas go down to look for their own people.
Brother
On that friday 16 zamas went down

On Saturday they also waited in vain

Christo de Klerk, CEO of Mine Rescue Services says they were only called in late on Saturday and went to the site first thing on Sunday morning.
Rescue services


Zamas are taking up more and more of Christo's teams' time. Just in 2016 they've already recovered the bodies of 24 zamas.
Rescue services


Meanwhile tensions on the surface at Langlaagte mounted. The trapped miners had now been underground for 11 days. Police arrested 7 of the zamas as they came out, making the others stay underground and relatives like Daroh panicked that time was running out to for injured zamas like his brother

Also, the newshounds had got word of the crisis by the sunday and two political leaders also put in an appearance, the mayor of Johannesburg, and the national minister of mining. The rescue team helped a few zamas to the top, but found no bodies. On Monday another sortie went down and they found one body.
Rescue services


On tuesday morning the search was called off. Daroh's brother was still missing.On tuesday night, a group of Zamas and relatives went down once more. They retrieved two bodies, one of them Daroh's brother Sibangani
Brother

Emma


Various role players have been asking for a long time to decriminalise the zamas or at least part of their activities, to try and regulate this seemingly unstoppable monster which is also also costing the economy an estimated R6 billion per annum.
Janet


The zamas argue that they'd rather endanger their own lives than become hijackers or armed robbers, but for now, the mining remains illegal.
Emma
Yes it is stealing but...
Mayor
We will close down the holes

On thursday the police started handing out pamphlets stating that FNB will be sealed off in two weeks time. Not even knowing if all the zamas involved in this disaster have been rescued already, it remains an open question as to how they can be sure that there is no one underground when they seal the shaft.
Mayor

Emma


And barely two days after the tragedy ended, Thabang and friends were headed down the same shaft again – they are hungry and there is no other way for them to earn money for bread....
Zama

Devi closing link



PROMO 10sec
How far would you go to feed your family? Would you illegally enter disused mineshafts and tunnel through partially collapsed crevaces, for a mere handful of rands?


PROMO 15sec
Desperate humans, crawling through the earth like burrowing termites...

Janet Love: The reality is you're talking about thousands of people...

People who are desperate to make a couple of hundred rands and feed their hungry families. Meet the Zamazamas.


PROMO 15sec
The Witwatersrand is literally crawling with young men desperate to strike gold...

Herman: How can anyone have sympathy for lawlessness, I'm not for lawlessness. I am for the rule of law.

Zamazamas... ruthless criminals or ordinary people trying to make a living?
